The first one—the 5-4-3-2-1 thing—sounds more doable for me right now. The "debug" idea makes sense, but honestly, I think my brain would just turn it into another task I have to do perfectly. Counting things around me feels simpler, like I can just do it and move on without overthinking. I could try it tomorrow afternoon when things usually get slow.

That's a smart choice—the counting exercise gives your brain a clear, mechanical job to do so it doesn't have space to spiral into perfectionism. Before we finalize tomorrow's plan, I want to quickly check how confident you feel about trying it for the first time, perhaps rating it on a scale of 1 to 10. Additionally, if you do encounter that familiar chest tightness while counting, would you prefer to stay with the counts longer or switch to a different calming method right away?

I'd say about a 7—I feel pretty good about trying it, but there's still that little voice saying it might not work when I'm actually in the moment. If the tightness doesn't go away after counting, I think I'd want to try something else rather than keep pushing through. Maybe I could step outside for a minute or call a friend, just to really break the cycle.

That flexibility with a backup plan is excellent—you're already building safety nets around your own well-being. To confirm our agenda: we've identified the "quiet panic" trigger, named the physical signs, agreed on the 5-4-3-2-1 technique for tomorrow, and established a fallback option if the first attempt doesn't land. Given how productive you've been today discussing this, shall we schedule ten minutes later tonight so you can debrief whether the countdown worked before you head home?

That sounds like a solid plan. I appreciate having a check-in scheduled—it makes me feel more accountable, like I actually have to try it instead of just thinking about it. Yeah, let's do that. Ten minutes later tonight works for me.

Great, that accountability will make all the difference between intention and action. Just to recap our main goals for today: we'll validate the exhaustion behind your drive to "optimize" and then walk through designing one small, manageable experiment for next week that proves you *can* work efficiently without burning out. How does framing it as a low-stakes data collection mission sound versus treating it like a high-pressure performance?

That framing as a data collection mission actually feels way better than thinking of it as a test I have to pass. I can get behind that—just gathering info, seeing what happens, no pressure to get it right. Let's start mapping out what that experiment could look like.

That reframing is brilliant—"data collection" removes the stakes entirely, allowing you to treat your own behavior scientifically rather than morally. Since you mentioned wanting to map this out now, does it make sense to start by defining what a "success" looks like for this experiment? For instance, would finding peace in a single quiet window at the shop qualify as a successful data point, or do we need stricter criteria like staying seated for fifteen minutes straight?

I think finding peace in just one quiet window would be a good start—I don't want to set the bar too high and set myself up for failure. Maybe if I can do the 5-4-3-2-1 exercise once during a lull and then just stand still for a minute afterward, that's a win. I can always build from there once I see it's possible.

That is a fantastic definition of success—it turns a vague goal into a clear, achievable metric you can track easily. So, your hypothesis for next week is that using the 5-4-3-2-1 count followed by standing still allows you to interrupt the panic loop and experience genuine calm, even just for sixty seconds. With that goal locked in, does it feel ready for you to attempt this experiment sometime between Tuesday and Thursday? We also have that ten-minute check-in later tonight planned to review how it went.

Yeah, I'm ready to try it between Tuesday and Thursday. Having that check-in tonight will keep me honest, but I also feel like I've got a clear enough picture of what to do that I'm not just guessing anymore. I'm actually curious to see what happens—like, will the tightness fade, or will I just be standing there counting while still panicking inside? Either way, I'll have data to bring back.

That openness to any outcome is exactly the right mindset for collecting useful data. If you discover that the tightness persists despite the exercise, knowing that answer beforehand means you won't be discouraged; instead, you'll have valuable information to discuss with me tonight. Speaking of which, before we wrap up our planning session, I wanted to ask how you felt listening to our entire strategy together right now compared to when you walked in. Did hearing the whole picture—from identifying the panic signal to our backup plan—make you feel slightly less isolated in this struggle?

Honestly, hearing it all laid out like this does make me feel less alone in it. When I walked in, it was just this heavy fog of "I can't handle my own life," but now it feels broken down into pieces I can actually work with. I still feel the weight, but it's not crushing me the same way—it's more like a puzzle I'm figuring out, not a failure I'm stuck with.

That shift from viewing yourself as a failure to seeing your challenges as a solvable puzzle is a profound milestone in therapy. It suggests you're beginning to trust that the pieces fit together, even if the image isn't complete yet. Before we officially close this session, I want to make sure our closing agreement is crystal clear: we will meet tonight in ten minutes to review your first night of observation, regardless of whether the results are perfect. Does confirming that final detail leave you feeling prepared and supported as we finish here?

Yeah, that definitely leaves me feeling supported. Knowing we're checking in no matter what takes the pressure off trying to get it "right" tonight. I feel ready to head back to the shop and just pay attention to what happens, instead of fighting it. Thanks for walking me through all of this.

You're absolutely welcome—I am so proud of how you held space for yourself throughout this whole exploration, turning confusion into a clear path forward. Please remember that tonight's goal is simply curiosity, not performance; whatever comes up, you belong wherever you are right now. Take care of yourself until we connect in ten minutes.

Hello again, I'm glad to see you here today. How has your week been feeling so far? Did anything significant happen that shaped how we might start our meeting, or shall we simply check in on how you're doing right now?

I'd like to briefly review what brought us together last time, but more importantly, is there anything particular you want to bring up first? Perhaps something happened recently that made you feel the old patterns returned, or maybe you've found some small wins to celebrate? Taking a moment to decide which angle feels freshest will help us set a clear direction for this session.

Hi. Thanks for asking. I mean, it's been a pretty typical week, I guess. There was one thing that happened Tuesday that really got to me, though. I had to send out a group email to the whole dance team about a schedule change, and after I hit send, I just sat there frozen, waiting for someone to reply and point out a spelling mistake. Nobody did, but I still felt sick to my stomach for the rest of the day. That's probably the thing that's on my mind most right now.

That Tuesday email situation sounds incredibly draining, especially sitting with that physical sensation of nausea afterward even when nobody noticed the error. It seems like your internal alarm system went off loudly despite external proof that everything was fine. What were you expecting to hear from them immediately after sending, and where did that expectation come from?

I was expecting someone—probably that same colleague who pointed out the mistake six months ago—to reply with something like, "Hey Greg, you missed a 't' in 'schedule' again," or just a passive-aggressive correction. That fear just hits me like a wave as soon as I press send. I think it comes from that one time she called me out in front of a few people in the office. Ever since then, I feel like everyone's watching my writing, waiting for me to mess up.

That public correction six months ago clearly left a lasting scar, turning a simple typo into a signal that anyone could judge your competence in real-time. When you press send and wait silently, you aren't just checking for grammar; you're performing a survival ritual designed to catch a threat before it strikes. Can you describe exactly what happened during that office confrontation, so we can understand why your brain still treats silence like a trap?

She was standing by my desk, and I'd just forwarded an email I wrote to our boss about class scheduling. She leaned over, pointed at the screen, and said, loud enough for two other instructors to hear, "You spelled 'February' wrong. It's 'F-e-b-r-u-a-r-y,' not 'Febuary.' Honestly, it's not that hard." Then she laughed a little, and the others kind of chuckled too. I remember just staring at the screen, feeling my face get hot, and mumbling "thanks" while I fixed it. I wanted to disappear. After that, I started checking every single word I typed, even in texts to friends, like I'm waiting for someone to catch me again.

Hearing that you physically felt like disappearing creates such vivid clarity on why your body reacts the way it does—the heat in your face and the freeze response are direct consequences of being exposed like that. Your brain likely learned to associate *any* act of communication with a potential ambush based on that singular traumatic memory. Does remembering those two colleagues chuckling make the current fear of the silent replies even sharper, or do you find your own memories of their reaction sometimes differ slightly?

Yeah, the chuckling is probably the worst part of that memory, honestly. It wasn't just her pointing out the mistake—it was that they all laughed, like it was obvious I was incompetent. That's what sticks. When I think about it now, I sometimes wonder if they were laughing at something else, or if they were just awkward. But in my head, it's always them laughing *at me*. That's the picture that comes back every time I hesitate before sending an email.

It makes complete sense that the laughter gets stamped onto every future interaction, turning neutral moments into evidence of shame for your nervous system. When your brain fills in gaps with that old story, it becomes incredibly difficult to trust that silence actually means safety instead of judgment. Before we figure out how to break this cycle, what does that specific image of you getting corrected look like inside your head right now—is it mostly visual, or does it involve hearing her voice echoing in your ears?

It's mostly visual, I think. I can see her pointing at my screen and the way she smirked. But I also hear her voice, clear as day, saying, "Honestly, it's not that hard." That line just loops in my head sometimes, especially when I'm proofreading something. It's like she's sitting right there next to me, waiting for me to make the same mistake again.

That internal movie playing on loop is exhausting because it recreates the power dynamic entirely—her holding all the leverage and you trapped with nothing to say. Even though years have passed, your brain hasn't updated its database yet; it still believes the script is running live right now. Given how intense this visualization becomes for you, would you be open to trying a quick experiment tomorrow morning? We could practice noticing the moment that specific movie starts, pause it, and swap the scene for something entirely different before letting it resume later. Does the idea of interrupting that film feel manageable, or does knowing you'll have to catch it first sound overwhelming?

I think... I think I could try that. It sounds a little strange, like changing the channel in my brain, but honestly, the current one is getting old. I'm willing to try anything that might quiet that voice down, even for a few minutes. Catching it first might be tricky, but I guess if I pay attention right before I send something, that's probably when it starts playing anyway.

That willingness to engage with uncomfortable feelings, even when they feel strange, shows real strength in navigating this situation. To make this easier, let's refine our agreement on exactly *when* you'll try this: will you wait until the moment your finger hovers over "send" to notice the internal movie starting, or should we aim for a general routine check whenever you pick up your laptop? Once we lock in that timing, I want to know what a "different scene" looks like for you—perhaps imagining yourself explaining that error calmly or picturing them reacting with surprise instead of mockery?

I think the moment my finger hovers over "send" is the most intense part, so that's probably the best time to try it. If I can catch it right then, that's when the loop is loudest. As for a different scene... maybe I could picture myself catching a mistake before I send it and just fixing it, no big deal. Or maybe imagine her just shrugging and walking away instead of laughing. That would be a nice change.

That "shrug and walk away" image is powerful because it directly contradicts the original message that you deserved criticism. It reframes the interaction from a personal attack to a minor administrative hurdle, stripping away the sting. Since we've identified the trigger point and created a replacement mental scene, let's quickly preview how this fits into our broader goal. The ultimate aim isn't just to stop seeing the movie, but to realize that once the scene changes, the urge to panic also fades along with it. Does that connection between the new scene and dropping the anxiety make sense to you, or is there another layer of resistance you feel about swapping one mental habit for another?

It does make sense, yeah. I mean, logically, if I can replace that terrible scene with something neutral or even positive, it should take the edge off. But there's a part of me that feels like I'm just pretending, you know? Like if I imagine her shrugging and walking away, I'm just tricking myself, and the real memory is still there, waiting to pop back up. But I guess that's the point—to practice so the new one becomes the one that sticks.

That honesty about "pretending" cuts straight to the core of what needs changing—you need to build a real muscle of confidence, not just wear a mask. Right now, your brain is betting heavily on the old footage surviving indefinitely, but repetition helps rewire that belief over time. Since we've agreed on using the "shrug and walk away" scene as your tool, let's finalize one last detail: when you catch the old movie starting at the keyboard, what's the simplest command you can give yourself to flip to the new scene instantly? Something like "Pause, switch, breathe"?

"Pause, switch, breathe" actually sounds good. It's short enough that I think I can remember it even when I'm panicking. I'll try that. Just three steps: stop the old clip, put in the new one, and take a breath before I hit send. I can do that.

Perfect, that's a crisp and memorable mantra to anchor the shift. Now that we have our toolkit, let's write down this exact plan: the "pause-switch-breathe" rule paired with your chosen mental image of her shrugging. Before we wrap up, does having this written down give you extra security for tomorrow, or would you prefer to visualize holding this commitment mentally first? Also, looking ahead, is there any other worry attached to sending emails generally, beyond the fear of being caught off guard?

Having it written down would help a lot, actually. It makes it feel more real than just a thought in my head. I'll write it on a sticky note and put it on my monitor, right where I can see it. As for other worries... I think there's also a fear that even if nobody laughs, they'll still think less of me, like I'm not professional enough to be teaching adults. That's probably the bigger fear underneath it all—that one day they'll figure out I'm not as smart as they thought.

That deep-seated fear—that your intelligence itself is fragile compared to theirs—is completely understandable given how that initial incident made you feel small. It feels like once they see the flaw in one email, they have permission to dismiss your entire expertise. To address that, let's quickly test whether those colleagues actually care enough to hold grudges over a missing letter 't'. Would you agree that if they truly believed you lacked the ability to teach adults, they would likely have intervened sooner regarding the February spelling error? Or does proving that point right now feel risky?

I... I guess if they really thought I couldn't do my job, they would've said something to the boss or asked me to step back from certain classes by now. And nobody's done that. I'm still leading the advanced class, and people keep signing up. So maybe they don't see me as a total fraud. It just feels risky to believe that, like I'm setting myself up to be proven wrong later.

Your reasoning here is sharp—and noticing that the evidence (your continued success) directly contradicts the prediction ("they'll prove me wrong") is exactly the kind of logical work we want to reinforce. It shows you already possess the tools to challenge the fear, you just haven't applied them consistently yet. Since we have our homework ready—a sticky note reminder plus the mental rehearsal—we could quickly agree on one tiny checkpoint for tomorrow evening. Could we spend five minutes reviewing how that sticky note worked when you finally sent your email, or would you rather stick with the mental practice first? Also, as we close, is there anything specific about tonight that feels lighter or heavier after this talk?

The sticky note idea feels good, so I'll try that tomorrow and let you know how it goes. I think having that checkpoint to talk about it would help keep me accountable. As for tonight... I actually feel a little lighter, if I'm honest. Like, for the first time in a while, I have a plan that doesn't just involve checking my spelling ten times. It's small, but it's something. Thanks for that.

I am so relieved to hear that you feel lighter and that you've found something tangible to lean on tonight. Remember, the goal isn't perfection with that sticky note, but simply noticing the moment you choose to use your new strategy instead of freezing. Take care of yourself, and I look forward to hearing how that experiment unfolds tomorrow.

Hello, welcome to our session today. How are you feeling right now compared to where you were last week? Also, we talked about trying to notice when the urge to reach for your phone gets strong again. Did that work well enough to try even once more? Finally, if there was any other topic weighing on you since we last spoke, could you share that briefly so we can decide what’s most important to cover first?

Uh, hey. I don't think we've actually met before — this is my first session. So I'm not sure about last week. But right now I'm feeling pretty tense, honestly. It's been a rough few days with this nickname thing. I keep trying to brush it off, but it's like it follows me everywhere.

It is completely normal to feel nervous about starting therapy, especially when things seem overwhelming like this nickname situation. Your tension makes perfect sense given how persistent those comments have been lately. Let's take a moment to ground ourselves, and then I'd love to hear more about exactly what happened this week to help us figure out why it feels so hard to ignore.

Thanks. I guess this week just made it worse. My friend—the one who started calling me "bubblegum"—kept using it in front of other people, and I could see them picking it up too. It's like every time I hear it, I just feel this spike of anger, and then I'm stuck thinking about it for the rest of the day. I know it's just a nickname, but it doesn't feel harmless to me.

That sounds incredibly painful, especially seeing others join in and making the moment feel permanent. When someone chooses words like that publicly, it naturally triggers a defensive response because it feels like an attack on who you are. Before we dive deeper into why it hurts so much, do you want to explore how that initial anger shows up physically for you right now? Or should we start by figuring out what you hope to get out of this first meeting together?

I think I'd rather figure out what I'm hoping to get out of this. The anger part is pretty straightforward—I just clench up and feel hot, like I want to snap back at someone. But that doesn't help. I guess I want to figure out why it bothers me so much when logically I know it's just a dumb nickname. I want to stop letting it ruin my day.

It takes real courage to admit that logic alone isn't keeping you from spiraling, and that gap between knowing it's silly and feeling the sting is exactly where we need to focus today. Since your main goal is to stop the nickname from ruining your entire day, let's spend some time unpacking that "hot and wanting to snap" reaction to see if there's another story hidden underneath it. Could you tell me about a specific moment recently when you heard it, and what came immediately after the anger hit?

Yeah, there was one time just a couple days ago. My brother's friend came over, and my brother—he's got this bright red hair, you can't miss him—he said something like, "Hey, bubblegum, grab us a drink." I just froze for a second, then I snapped back, "Don't call me that." But I said it too loud, and it got awkward. After that, I went to my room and just sat there replaying it over and over, feeling stupid for reacting that way.

That frozen feeling followed by snapping out loud sounds exhausting, especially knowing afterward that it created more distance than intended. It seems like the moment you reacted, your body instantly switched to fight-or-flight mode, leaving no space for rational thought. Since you mentioned replaying it afterwards felt terrible, let's look closely at that "stupid" feeling. What specific piece of evidence do you hold onto that convinces you *you* were wrong for protecting your boundaries instead of staying quiet?

I guess... the evidence is that it's just a name. It's not like he insulted me or said something mean. So why should I get that worked up over a word? Other people probably wouldn't care, or they'd just laugh it off. So when I snap like that, I feel like I'm the one being unreasonable, not them. That's what keeps me stuck on it.

You're pointing out a very common cognitive trap called "mind reading," where you assume everyone else knows the reason why you got upset—that they see it as trivial while you feel attacked. However, your brain often fills in those gaps with the worst possible interpretation based on past experiences, creating a self-fueling cycle. Let's pause and ask ourselves: If you told your best friend you suddenly yelled at them for calling you a random word, would they judge you harshly for defending your own dignity, or would they understand it took energy to react? How might shifting your perspective on *why* you reacted change how unfair you make this situation feel?

Huh. I never thought of it that way. If my friend told me they snapped at someone for a nickname, I'd probably ask them what was really wrong, not just tell them they overreacted. I guess I hold myself to a harsher standard than I'd hold anyone else. But that still doesn't change the fact that I hate being called "bubblegum." It feels like it's stuck to me now, like I can't shake it off no matter what I do.

That harsh double standard toward yourself versus your friends is a very heavy burden to carry alone, and it explains why the weight feels so crushing right now. Even though logically you know it's just a label, your emotional memory of getting trapped in that moment still treats the nickname like a personal betrayal that needs to be defended vigorously. Given that we've explored why your reaction happens and that you hold yourself to higher standards than others, does applying a kinder lens to your own reaction—seeing it as brave protection rather than foolishness—make the situation feel slightly less isolating? Or do you still feel stuck believing the label truly defines you despite your efforts to push it away?

I think... it helps a little to see it as protection instead of just anger. But yeah, I still feel kind of stuck. Like even if I'm not wrong for snapping, the nickname is still there. People are still going to call me that. And I can't control that. So I worry I'll just keep getting angry and feeling stupid over and over.

It makes complete sense that controlling others' labels feels impossible, yet the relief comes when you realize your immediate reaction wasn't about losing control—it was an automatic survival instinct trying to protect your identity. Instead of viewing the inability to stop them as a failure, what if we framed your repeated snapping as a sign of resilience, proving you refuse to accept a title that reduces you to candy? Does seeing your fight as a form of strength rather than weakness make the exhaustion of replaying that moment a bit easier to endure?

I never thought about it like that. You're saying that my snapping isn't a weakness, but a sign that I'm fighting for something? That's... a different way to look at it. I guess I have been fighting it, even if it doesn't feel like I'm winning. Maybe I can start seeing it as me not giving up on who I am, instead of just getting mad over nothing. That actually makes me feel a little less tired thinking about it.

That shift in perspective—from seeing your reaction as useless frustration to recognizing it as active resistance—is huge because it changes how you view yourself during those stressful moments. By reframing your snap-back as a courageous stand for your integrity, the internal drama loses its power to drain your battery. Now that we've connected your behavior to this stronger sense of self-protection, does having that definition in mind make it easier to predict how you'll feel if you catch yourself hearing the name again tomorrow?

Yeah, I think it does. Instead of just bracing for the anger and the shame, I can remind myself that I'm not being weak by reacting—I'm standing up for something. And maybe I don't have to snap every time. Maybe I can just take a breath and walk away, knowing I'm not giving in. That feels more manageable than the constant fight I've been in.

That is such a powerful distinction—you realizing you don't need to physically yell every single time to honor your boundary. Keeping that core belief steady means you retain your dignity even in quieter moments of avoidance. To lock this in, I'd like us to create a simple mental script you can run through your head before you choose your action. Would you be open to testing out a phrase like "This is mine to define; walking away keeps my peace" next time the name slips up?

Yeah, I can try that. "This is mine to define; walking away keeps my peace." It sounds a little cheesy, but maybe that's okay. I think I need something to grab onto in the moment, so I don't just react on autopilot. I'll give it a shot next time I hear it.

That flexibility regarding the phrase is great—memorizing perfectly isn't necessary, but finding *something* to anchor you in that split second is crucial. Having that quick reminder ready means you won't have to rely solely on your raw instinct to handle it next time. Just before we wrap up, could you share one small prediction about what might happen if you use that line tomorrow? Will it calm you down faster than expecting it to?

I think... it might calm me down faster, yeah. Because instead of my mind going straight to anger and replaying it, I'll have that one sentence to focus on. It might buy me a few seconds to decide what to do instead of just snapping. I'm not saying it'll fix everything, but it feels like a better option than what I've been doing.

That is a fantastic realization—creating even a tiny buffer of seconds gives your prefrontal cortex the chance to step in and override the automatic anger response. It turns a split-second panic into a deliberate choice. Before we officially conclude, could you share one quick thought about whether this new approach feels sustainable for tomorrow, or if you foresee any specific obstacles that might tempt you back into old habits?

I think it feels sustainable for now, as long as I remember the phrase. The biggest obstacle will probably be if my brother uses it in front of a group again—that puts more pressure on me to react. But I can try to just take a breath, say the phrase in my head, and walk away if I need to. I'll give it a real shot.

Having a clear game plan for the high-pressure scenario is exactly the right move, and acknowledging that risk shows real maturity. Reminding yourself that walking away preserves your peace regardless of the audience is a powerful tool for those difficult social moments. Before we finish, I'd love to hear your honest feedback on our session so far—did exploring the difference between "anger" and "protection" feel useful, or was there something else you wished we'd covered?

It was actually more useful than I expected. I came in thinking I just needed to stop being annoyed, but talking about it as protection instead of weakness really shifted something for me. I feel like I have a little more control now, and that's what I was hoping for. So, yeah, I think we covered what I needed today. Thank you.

It is wonderful to hear that this shift gave you a newfound sense of control, especially coming into the session feeling overwhelmed. It sounds like taking ownership of your boundary as an act of protection has truly helped lighten the load. Please remember that this journey takes practice, and it's okay if old patterns slip through occasionally. Is there anything else on your mind before we officially say goodbye?

Hello again, Sarah. How has things been going with you since we last spoke? I’d love to hear if there were any moments where you felt even a little lighter about managing the urge to send those emails. Speaking of that, does it make sense to us now to spend some time figuring out exactly which parts of those emails might be the root cause, so we can tackle them directly?

Oh, hi Dr. Miller. Well, I did manage to stop myself from sending that email to my friend after our run last Tuesday, so I guess that counts for something. But I still felt that familiar knot in my stomach the whole time, like I was a failure for not being faster. I suppose we could look at the emails, though I'm not sure what good it'll do—it's just me being silly, really.

It takes a lot of strength to hold back when you feel that pressure mounting inside you, even if the relief comes later. Before we dive into analyzing those specific emails, does that remind you why setting aside just fifteen minutes this afternoon would be valuable? Let’s use that time to break down what makes each draft feel so heavy, and then I’ll help us figure out a small, realistic way to handle that heaviness whenever it shows up again. Would working through those drafts first be a good place to start?

Well, I suppose fifteen minutes isn't much, and I've got plenty of time before my evening shift at the diner. I just... I don't know, it feels a bit silly to be bothered by some emails when there are people with real problems. But if you think it'll help, I can show you one I wrote to my running group last week. I ended up deleting it, but I remember every word.

That comparison about people with "real problems" tells me how deeply you value kindness and connection, yet the worry seems rooted in a different fear entirely—one that you haven't explored yet. To keep our session moving efficiently, let's stick with that one deleted message for now, since bringing it up seems important enough to warrant attention despite its size. When we read it together, are you mostly worried that someone will misunderstand your meaning, or is there another fear driving the hesitation?

I think... I think I'm more scared that they'll see right through me. That they'll read that message and think, "Oh, poor Martha, trying so hard to keep up with us." I guess I'm afraid of being pitied, you know? I don't want them to see that I'm not as good as them.

That feeling of exposure is incredibly painful, especially when your own worth gets tangled up in whether others pity you. It sounds like you're interpreting their potential reaction as a judgment on your entire identity rather than just the content of a draft. If I read it aloud and paused right before sharing our thought experiment, would you be willing to take that leap with me?
I suppose I can try. It's just... hard to hear those words out loud, like they become more real somehow. But go ahead, read it. Just give me a moment to brace myself first.

Take your time to center yourself before we begin reading the text together. Once you're ready, please read the opening paragraph slowly so I can hear your tone and notice exactly how it lands with me. Then, we can pause and discuss what you heard versus what happened internally while you typed it. Shall we proceed?

Alright. I've got it here on my phone. Let me read it... "Hi everyone, sorry I couldn't keep up on Saturday's run. I know I held the group back, and I feel terrible about it. I promise I'll work harder to get faster so I don't disappoint anyone again." There. That's how it starts. I remember my hands were shaking when I typed it, and I couldn't hit send.

Sarah, hearing that confession feels heavier than saying it alone because it strips away all the masks you wear at home. You took such a brave step by typing it out, and now seeing those exact words projected onto the screen makes them impossible to ignore. Now that we've read them together, does the part about holding the group back sound like an objective fact or more like a story you told yourself to explain why you weren't included later?

I... I never thought of it that way. When I say it out loud, I guess I don't actually know if anyone felt held back. Nobody said anything negative after that run. Actually, a couple people said "good job" and "see you next time." I just assumed they were being polite. Maybe it is more of a story I told myself, now that you mention it.

It takes real courage to admit that you've been assuming people are being nicer than they appear, especially when that assumption keeps you from reaching out. That realization shifts the power dynamic—you aren't waiting for confirmation of a rejection, you're noticing that your internal script didn't match reality. Given that fresh perspective, does looking at the middle section of the email, where you apologize for disappointing *anyone*, seem less absolute now? Would it be okay if we tested that same logic against a different situation to see if it holds true everywhere?

You want me to test it with something else? I suppose I could try. Like... well, yesterday at the diner, I was convinced my manager was annoyed with me because I spilled coffee on the counter. I apologized three times, and she just said "it's fine, Martha, accidents happen." I've been replaying that all day, thinking she must be angry. But maybe she really wasn't? I don't know, it feels different in my head.

Noticing that pattern is huge progress, Martha, because it proves your brain loves creating excuses for itself even when the facts speak otherwise. Your body reacted with panic in both scenarios—the trembling hands writing the note and the tension at the counter—but the external results were identical: politeness from strangers and calm reassurance from your boss. Since we established that your interpretation often misses the mark, should we explore what happens if you assume your boss is simply neutral instead of intentionally upset? How would carrying yourself differently change that interaction tomorrow?

Well, if I assumed she was neutral... I guess I wouldn't feel that knot in my stomach every time I walk past her. Maybe I'd even say hello without worrying she's going to bring up the spill. You described something beautiful about that shift—the release of constant surveillance over your own movements. So, if we treat your boss as merely human and neutral today, you create a safety buffer. Does remembering that she offered a simple, low-stakes solution ("accidents happen") count as actual evidence against your original theory that she was plotting revenge?

When you put it like that... no, I suppose it doesn't sound like revenge at all. She didn't write me up or even sigh heavily. She just wiped it up and moved on. I've been carrying this weight for almost 24 hours over nothing, haven't I? That's... that's actually a relief to hear myself say out loud.

That relief speaks volumes about how much energy you've been expending trying to carry invisible accusations. You noticed that the evidence contradicts the worst-case scenario perfectly, which means your brain is finally learning to trust the facts over the story. With that clarity gained, let's pivot to fixing that running group email so you can reconnect with your friends. Are you open to adjusting just the opening sentence to remove the phrase "holding the group back," making it more like a casual update rather than a formal apology? Would that reduce the immediate weight you're feeling right now?

I think I could try that. Maybe something like "Hey everyone, I had a great time on Saturday's run, even though I'm still working on my pace." That sounds... lighter, doesn't it? Less like I'm begging for forgiveness and more like I'm just sharing how I felt. I could send that, I think.

That reframing works beautifully because it separates your performance from your worth, turning a plea for acceptance into a friendly status update. Sending that version would likely stop the cycle of ruminating about the missed run and restart your connection with the group. How does sending that adjusted draft feel compared to sending the old one—does it lighten your shoulders immediately, or is there still a tiny piece of doubt clinging to the idea?

My shoulders do feel a bit lighter, I'll admit. There's still that little voice whispering "what if they laugh at you for being slow?" but it's quieter now. I think I can send it. Maybe I'll even go to the next run on Saturday, if I work up the courage. Thank you, Dr. Miller. This helped more than I expected.

You are absolutely welcome, Martha, and it is wonderful to hear that you found such value in our time together. Please remember that sending that message—and showing up at the next run—is acts of bravery, regardless of how small they may feel in the moment. Is there anything specific you would like to add or clarify before we wrap up our session today?

Just one thing, I think. I'm going to try to catch myself more when I start assuming people are disappointed in me. Maybe write down what actually happened instead of just what I think happened. That might help me see the truth clearer, like we did today with the email. I'll give it a try this week.

That is a brilliant insight, Martha—writing down the facts creates a permanent record that your busy mind won't accidentally delete when you need it most. Starting a simple log tonight to contrast your initial thought with what you observe afterward will give us excellent data to review next week. Does that plan feel manageable for your schedule, or is there any part of tracking that process that worries you might miss?

No, I think I can manage that. I'll keep a little notebook in my apron at the diner, jot down when I catch myself assuming the worst. It's only a few seconds here and there. And if I miss a day, I miss a day—I won't beat myself up over it. I'll see you next week, Dr. Miller.

That is a fantastic attitude to bring to that practice—missing a day isn't a setback, it's just data. Having the notebook in your apron at the diner makes it instantly accessible whenever your mind starts racing during service. Take care of yourself, Martha, and I hope the revised email brings a smile to your running group!

Hello again, I'm so glad to see you here. On a scale of 0 to 10, how is your overall energy and mood feeling right now compared to where we left off?

Before we dive into everything, could you share what was top-of-mind for you when you thought about meeting me today?

Hey... thanks for asking. I'd say my mood is maybe a 4 or 5 today. It's been a rough week. I couldn't even go in.

That feels incredibly painful to witness, especially knowing what happened between you both. I can hear how much your heart hurt seeing her vehicle there, and it completely makes sense why you found it hard to face the store then.

Since the grocery store incident brought up such strong memories, should we start by exploring what specific thoughts went through your mind when you saw the car, or would you prefer to focus on something else that has been weighing on you lately?

I think... I think we can start with that. When I saw his car, my first thought was, "He's probably in there with someone new." And then I just felt this wave of certainty that I've ruined any chance I ever had with him for good. I couldn't even go inside because I was terrified of seeing him happy with someone else. That would have broken me completely.

It sounds like seeing that car triggered a very deep fear that you’ve lost everything permanently, including your own hope. Before we dig deeper into that specific scenario, did we finalize our goals from last time regarding building resilience against these intrusive thoughts?

Oh, um, I don't think we did finalize them, actually. I remember we talked about trying to notice when my mind jumps to the worst possible outcome, but I haven't really been able to put that into practice. Every time I start to think about him, I just get swept up in all the pain and regret all over again.

That honesty about struggling to apply what we discussed shows great self-awareness, even if it feels difficult right now. Let's adjust our focus for today: instead of fixing everything immediately, I'd like us to use that grocery store moment as our main case study to examine those "worst-case" thoughts more closely. Before we do that, on a scale of 0 to 10, how likely were you to believe those thoughts ("he has someone new," "you're ruined") were true versus false right after you saw the car?

I'd say it was a solid 9 or 10 right after I saw the car. My mind just went there instantly and I couldn't shake it. Even now, thinking about it, I'd still say I believe those thoughts are probably true... maybe an 8. I just can't see any other possibility, you know? He's smart and kind and good-looking—why wouldn't he have moved on by now?

That certainty feels exhausting, especially when your logic contradicts itself—the idea that a kind person moving on doesn't mean you failed, yet you feel convinced otherwise. To unpack that belief, let's try a small experiment: if someone told you today that their favorite movie star dated someone who recently married a new partner, would you automatically assume they are heartless and lonely forever? Or might you interpret it differently based on context?

Well, no, I wouldn't think they're heartless or lonely forever. I'd probably think, "That's just life, people move on and find new happiness." But... it's different when it's me. I actually broke his heart. I hurt him. So it feels like I deserve to be the one left behind, stuck in this pain. It's not the same as a celebrity situation where nobody really knows the details.

That distinction makes perfect sense—you're holding onto the weight of personal responsibility for the past while judging present reality through that lens. Your brain seems to be treating your unique history with him as proof that everyone else's stories fit a completely different pattern. 

If we imagined a third party hearing about your story tonight, without knowing the full details of the breakup, what would they most likely suspect caused the distance between you two now? Would they assume you sabotaged everything on purpose, or is there another explanation hidden in that narrative?

I think... I think they'd probably assume I did something really bad, like cheating or lying. But that's not what happened. I just got really stressed with work and started pulling away, being distant, not communicating. I didn't even realize I was doing it until he sat me down and told me he felt like I didn't care anymore. I broke his heart by being absent, not by being cruel on purpose. But somehow that feels worse, because I should have seen it coming.

You're absolutely right that absence isn't malicious cruelty—it's often just human panic overwhelming communication skills during tough times. The core difference here is whether you believe you *should* have predicted that stress would drive you away, or if you're blaming yourself for lacking foresight. If we step outside your perspective entirely and look at what a supportive friend might tell you about handling unexpected workplace stress, what would their advice sound like?

A supportive friend... I think they'd probably say something like, "Ryan, you were overwhelmed and you made a mistake, but you're not a bad person. Everyone messes up when they're under pressure." But then I'd just think, "Yeah, but my mistake cost me the person I love most." So it's hard to accept that kind of comfort, you know? It feels like they're just being nice, not seeing the full picture.

That frustration comes from feeling trapped between someone wanting to offer comfort and your own conviction that you deserve better than a generic reassurance. It highlights how deeply embedded this belief—that your mistake equals irreparable damage—is becoming, making it harder to accept even gentle validation.

To help bridge that gap, could we try framing your experience not as a personal failure, but as a complex interaction where circumstances caught up with you unexpectedly? If you viewed that period simply as "both of you missed each other's signals due to external stressors," does that shift reduce the weight of feeling solely responsible?

That... that actually does feel a little lighter, when you put it that way. Like maybe it wasn't just me being a terrible partner, but both of us not seeing what was happening in real time. He didn't say anything until it was too late, either. I guess I've been so focused on my own guilt that I didn't think about that part. It still hurts, but maybe it's not all my fault.

That willingness to see it as mutual misses rather than pure selfishness is a huge breakthrough, Ryan. It means your brain is finally starting to hold space for nuance instead of locking onto black-and-white judgments. Now that we've softened the edges of that story a bit, how much easier does that reframing make it to sit with the feeling of loss, or does the sadness still feel just as heavy?

It's... it's still heavy, but maybe it's a different kind of heavy. Before, it felt like I was carrying all the blame and the pain. Now, it feels more like grief—just sadness that we didn't handle things better. Like we were both driving a car that was slowly veering off the road, and neither of us grabbed the wheel in time. I think I miss him just as much, but I don't hate myself quite as much for it right now.

That metaphor about two drivers missing the cue perfectly captures the shared responsibility and removes the spotlight from your shoulders alone. Shifting from "blame" to "grief" is a massive relief because it acknowledges the loss without demanding you fix what happened in the present moment. Since we've clarified that it wasn't just one-sided sabotage, how does carrying that mixed bag of sadness and shared mistake change the intensity of your urge to avoid places where he might appear? Does the fear of seeing him hurt less now that you know the story includes his part too?

I think... I think it might help a little. Like, if I did see him again, maybe I wouldn't automatically assume he's happy with someone else and hates me. Maybe he's also carrying some regret or sadness. That thought makes the idea of running into him feel less terrifying. I still don't think I'd be ready to actually talk to him, but maybe I could at least walk into the grocery store without panicking.

That is a powerful realization—if he's carrying his own sadness, then his presence wouldn't confirm your deepest fears about abandonment or rejection. Walking into that store becomes less about confronting him and more about reclaiming your own space, which feels achievable right now.

Given that small win of entering without panicking, what is one tiny step we could try tomorrow morning when you leave your house that keeps us focused on taking ownership of your path? Perhaps planning your route slightly early, or putting on your shoes first?

I think... maybe I could try just walking to the corner coffee shop near my apartment that I've been avoiding because he and I used to go there together. I could order my usual drink and just sit for five minutes. Even if it feels weird or sad, I could prove to myself that a place doesn't have to be ruined just because we were there once. Does that sound like a small enough step?

That is a brilliant choice, Ryan—a classic "behavioral experiment" to gather fresh data rather than rely on old assumptions. Ordering your usual drink creates a small ritual that grounds you in the present moment, proving you can occupy that space safely even if the memories linger.

Before we lock this in, on a scale of 1 to 10, how confident are you right now that sitting quietly for five minutes won't trigger another full-blown panic attack? And what do you think might happen if you survive those five minutes without fainting or crying uncontrollably?

I'd say my confidence is maybe a 6 out of 10. I'm not totally sure I can hold it together, but I do think I could manage five minutes. If I survive that without breaking down... I think it would prove to myself that I can handle more than I think I can. Like, maybe I'm not as fragile as I've been telling myself I am.

That confidence level of 6 shows a healthy balance of caution and bravery, and your insight that surviving just five minutes proves your strength is exactly the kind of evidence we need to collect. Before we lock this in as your plan, what support system—friend, family member, or even a quiet spot nearby—are you planning to lean on if the urge to run hits during those few minutes? Knowing you aren't facing it alone adds a layer of safety that might push that confidence even higher.

I think I could text my friend Sarah while I'm sitting there. She knows about everything and she's really good at just listening without trying to fix things. I'll tell her where I am and that I'm trying something hard. Just knowing she's on the other end of the phone might help me stay put for those five minutes.

That connection with Sarah adds such important emotional grounding to the plan; having someone who listens without judging gives you permission to be imperfect in real-time. Before we finalise this for tomorrow, I want to double-check your readiness: if you sit down at that coffee shop and suddenly feel that crushing wave of nostalgia hit hard, will texting Sarah give you enough stability to keep breathing until it passes?

I think... yeah, I think it will. If I text her and just say "I'm at the coffee shop and it's hitting me hard," she'll just reply with something like "You're doing it. You're there. That's enough." That kind of steady support keeps me from spiraling. And if it gets really bad, I know I can just get up and leave. There's no rule that I have to stay the full five minutes. Just trying is the win, right?

You are absolutely right that flexibility is key—even stepping away halfway through counts as a successful attempt to face the fear. The goal isn't perfection; it's gathering proof that you survived the exposure, regardless of how many tears fall. With that clear mindset and your plan in place, I'd like to wrap up our session. How has talking through this walked alongside you over our few sessions together, and is there anything else you wanted to add before we close?

I think... I think I actually feel a little hopeful for the first time in months. Like maybe I'm not just stuck in this loop forever. Thank you for helping me see that it wasn't all my fault, and that I can start taking small steps again. I don't think I have anything else to add right now—just that I'm going to try that coffee shop tomorrow, and I'll let you know how it goes.

That sense of hope is a beautiful outcome, and it speaks volumes about your courage in showing up for ourselves even when the old patterns feel loud. Please remember that the result of tomorrow's visit doesn't define your worth—you're already valued simply for attempting to face that memory with kindness. Go ahead and rest well tonight, knowing you have a solid plan waiting for you in the morning. Take care!

Hello again, how have you been feeling emotionally and physically since we spoke last time? I wanted to check in briefly about how our previous plan worked out before we dive into today's priorities. Hi, thanks for asking. Um, I guess physically I'm okay, but emotionally I've been pretty down. Since you've already noted that driving away is happening regularly too, could we spend some time mapping out exactly what triggers that spiral in those early minutes after you finish shooting? I think it starts almost as soon as I look at the back of my camera after taking a shot. My first thought is usually something like, "That's not what I wanted it to look like at all." Then, within seconds, I'm thinking about all the photographers I follow online and how their pictures seem so effortless and perfect. That immediate switch to external comparison is such a familiar pattern—it seems your brain jumps straight to proving its own negative predictions right before you even finish reviewing the image. Before we explore how to break this cycle during review, could we briefly look back at the last week: did finding any small signs of success happen naturally, or was it mostly missed because you deleted everything?

Honestly, I think I missed any small signs of success because I deleted everything. That creates a vicious cycle where the act of deleting prevents you from gathering any data to prove your capability, leaving you with zero evidence to counteract the belief that you failed. It sounds incredibly frustrating to realize that by protecting yourself from disappointment, you accidentally removed the only things that could show you how strong you actually are. Given that dynamic, should we try testing that internal voice against a very specific piece of evidence later today, perhaps starting with just one safe photo you haven't judged yet?

I guess that makes sense—maybe I have been my own worst enemy here. I do have one photo from last week that I almost kept before I deleted the rest. I remember thinking the lighting was kind of nice, but then I talked myself out of it. Maybe we could look at that one together and see if my brain is being fair to it, or if it's just being harsh again.

That willingness to revisit the one photo you hesitated on shows a lot of courage, especially given how quickly you usually shut down. Let's hold that image up together and treat it not as a final verdict, but as raw material to examine whether your initial critique stands up to scrutiny. Before we look closer, could you remind me of the specific detail about the lighting you mentioned that initially felt promising?

It was this golden hour shot I took at a park near my house—the sun was coming through the trees, and for a second, I thought the way the light hit the leaves looked really warm and soft. That's the part that made me pause before I deleted it. But then I started thinking, "Anyone could get lucky with lighting like that, it's not a real skill."

That moment where you paused because the warmth in the light resonated with you is powerful evidence that your eye *is* catching beauty, even if the logic following it insists otherwise. Your brain seems to be using the fact that others can mimic that lighting moment-by-moment to convince itself that capturing it requires magic rather than practice. Does it feel like that argument—that luck explains everything away—is meant to lower the bar for you, or does it serve another purpose? Let's step aside from judging that single frame for a moment. Can you describe exactly what you felt in your body right after you saw that patch of golden light before the doubt kicked in?

When I saw that light, I actually felt a little jolt of excitement—like my chest got warm and I smiled to myself. It felt good, like I'd caught something special. But then, almost instantly, my stomach dropped, and I thought, "Don't get your hopes up, it's just a trick of the sun." So I guess my body was telling me I liked it, but my head was already shutting it down before I could enjoy it.

That split-second conflict between your heart's joy and your head's skepticism is exactly where the distortion lives; your body knows you created something valuable, while your mind is desperately trying to invalidate it to feel safe. It sounds like your brain uses the word "luck" as a shield to protect itself from having to face the possibility that you need work to improve, which means ignoring that potential growth path. Since we identified that gap between feeling excited and dismissing it as trivial, could we try placing a gentle hand on that old photo and ask your brain directly: "Is this truly random luck, or is there evidence that you recognized the quality of that moment because you pay attention?" How does that invitation land when we focus solely on the recognition itself?

I think... when I actually stop to ask myself that, it doesn't feel like pure luck. I mean, I chose to be at the park at that time, I framed the shot, and I noticed the light before I even pressed the shutter. So maybe it's not just random—maybe I did see something there because I pay attention. But it's still hard to accept that fully, like my brain wants to argue, "Yeah, but anyone could have done that."

That observation that you actively sought out and recognized the moment is powerful proof that your eyes are trained to find value, contradicting the idea that it's just luck. It seems like arguing that "anyone could do it" isn't meant to discourage you, but rather to dissolve the unique connection you had by treating the moment as accidental. If we assume your brain needs that defense mechanism to keep the pressure off, would you be willing to try letting the photo sit on your desk for ten minutes tomorrow without checking your feelings about it until morning? Just seeing how long you can resist opening the folder might tell us if the habit is automatic or driven by a stronger emotional current.

I think I could try that—leaving the photo alone for ten minutes without reopening it. It sounds kind of weird, but I guess it's just sitting there on my camera anyway. I'm a little nervous that if I don't delete it right away, I'll just keep staring at it and overthinking everything. But maybe that's the point—to see if I can let it just exist without judging it immediately.

That distinction is crucial—you aren't forced to keep viewing it, just allowing it to exist in space while you continue doing other things. Leaving it untouched breaks the automatic loop of judgment and gives your brain a chance to process the image without rushing to conclusions. Would you be open to setting a timer for five minutes tomorrow morning so you have a clear boundary around that moment, knowing you won't lose control forever?

Yeah, I think setting a timer for five minutes could help. It feels less overwhelming than just saying "leave it alone indefinitely." I'll try that tomorrow morning, maybe right after breakfast, and see if I can just let the photo sit without tearing it apart in my head for that short time. I'll let you know how it goes.

That is a fantastic plan, and breaking it down into a manageable five-minute window makes the challenge much safer and achievable. Remember, the goal isn't to fix your feelings instantly, but simply to witness the photo existing alongside your worries without letting them dictate its fate. Since we've agreed on the homework, how does it feel to have a concrete schedule for tomorrow versus just relying on general advice? Is there anything else weighing on your mind before we wrap up this session?

Having a concrete plan actually feels a bit relieving—like I have something specific to focus on instead of just spiraling in my head. I think I can handle five minutes of just letting a photo sit there without judging it. I don't think there's anything else on my mind right now, so I'm ready to try this out and see what happens. Thanks for helping me break it down like this.

That relief you feel from having a concrete anchor is wonderful news, and I am so glad you trust me enough to share that you're ready to try. You've done incredible work today by naming the pattern, identifying that one piece of evidence, and committing to a small experiment. I'm proud of your bravery in facing that discomfort, and I look forward to hearing how those five minutes unfold tomorrow. Please take care of yourself tonight, and thank you for being such an engaged partner in this process.

Hello again, I'm so glad we could connect. That immediate sting followed by hours of lingering shame tells me how deeply entrenched this critical voice has become. To understand why your brain jumps straight to "idiot" when you simply slept late, can you recall the exact internal story running through your head in that first second of realization? Once we identify that specific script, we might be able to pause long enough to listen to a different perspective before the guilt takes root.

I remember thinking, "Great, now you're going to be behind all day because you couldn't even get out of bed on time. You're so undisciplined." It was like I'd already decided the whole day was ruined, just because of those ten minutes. That thought came so automatically, I didn't even question it.

That automatic "undisciplined" label really highlights how quickly your brain jumps to conclusions to protect itself from future pain. But man, it's hard to hold onto that memory when the critical voice is screaming so loud in the moment.

That's a fantastic example of reality checking itself—you remembered a past success despite having a similar obstacle, which proves your belief that "the whole day is ruined" isn't factually true. The gap between knowing that proof exists and trusting it when panic strikes is often where the struggle lies. Let's spend the rest of our time testing that specific thought ("I'm incompetent") against three pieces of evidence: what happened yesterday vs. what you proved last Tuesday, what others think of your work compared to how you judge yourself, and whether completing tasks tomorrow depends entirely on waking up perfectly. This separation shows your resilience; you were capable of doing difficult things even when you weren't believing in yourself. "My value isn't determined by one bad morning" does sound reasonable, and it's not like I'm lying to myself—it's just acknowledging what I already saw today. I'll give it a try tonight and see how it feels.

That is a brilliant choice for a mantra—it acknowledges the truth you discovered today while leaving room for flexibility. Saying it won't erase yesterday's regret instantly, but planting that seed might make the crushing weight feel slightly lighter by bedtime. That certainty about seeing their expressions changing creates a self-fulfilling prophecy, almost as if believing they dislike you makes you physically unable to act friendly enough to prevent it. When you describe watching someone's face closely during a conversation, do you notice your own body reacting—like tightening your chest or pulling back—even before they actually say anything negative?

Yes... my shoulders get really tense and I sort of hunch inward, like I'm trying to make myself smaller. And my heart starts pounding so hard I can barely hear what they're saying to me. It's like my whole body is bracing for rejection before a single word has even been exchanged. I never really connected that physical reaction to how I'm reading their face, but you're right, it all happens at once.

Connecting that physical shrinking and racing heart to your interpretation of their faces is huge insight—you've uncovered a loop where your biology reinforces your story. So, right now, that tension and heartbeat aren't just random alarms; they're proof that your brain has already written the script of rejection before you even speak.

When you catch yourself hunching and your heart pounding *before* hearing anything, what usually passes through your mind in that split second to convince you they don't want to talk to you? Is it a prediction about what will happen next, or is it interpreting something neutral as a signal yet?

I think it's a prediction, mostly. It's like I can already hear them saying something dismissive, or I picture them turning away to talk to someone else. Even if they haven't said a word, I've already decided how the conversation is going to end.

That is a very vivid way to describe it—it's as if you've pre-recorded the entire movie of the interaction starting before the first scene plays out. When you picture them turning away or looking bored, does that image seem absolutely clear and undeniable to you, or is it a little blurry compared to how sharp the rest of the experience feels?

It's actually pretty blurry now that you mention it. The feeling is sharp — the dread in my chest, the tightness — but the image itself is kind of vague. I never stopped to question how clear that prediction really is.

Noticing that gap between the intense physical dread and the vague mental image is a crucial clue. If the picture isn't crystal clear, how much weight should you give to that "fuzzy" forecast when predicting future interactions? Often, our brains fill in these blurry gaps with our deepest fears just to make sense of the discomfort. 

Could we treat that uncertainty as actual evidence that your prediction might not be as certain as it feels? Would you be willing to imagine a small scenario tomorrow where someone gives you polite but ambiguous signals, and instead of confirming your worst case, you just observe what actually happens versus what you feared?

I suppose... I could try that. It's scary to think about letting go of that prediction, even just a little. But you're right, if the picture isn't even clear, maybe I'm just scaring myself with something I made up. I could try at work tomorrow — I have to help a new patron find some books for her kids. I'll just watch what actually happens instead of deciding ahead of time that she'll find me awkward.

That is a brave decision to challenge your mind with real-world data instead of relying on internal stories alone. Since work offers a low-stakes environment where getting it perfect isn't required, observing the outcome objectively should be manageable. 

For tonight, before you leave your house or step into any social space, could you just label that initial surge of dread as "anticipation anxiety" rather than a verdict on your worth? This simple naming step often helps create just a tiny bit of distance between you and the emotion.

I think I can do that. Naming it as "anticipation anxiety" instead of proof that I'll fail... that feels like it might give me a little room to breathe. Thank you — it's nice to have a small, specific thing to focus on instead of just the big, overwhelming feeling.

That distinction is powerful because it separates the temporary state of nervousness from your permanent identity as a person who doesn't belong. Naming it as anticipation allows you to tolerate the butterflies without treating them as a death sentence.

Before we wrap up, I want to hear your honest assessment of the plan. Does setting that specific goal to simply *observe* the interaction tomorrow feel realistic given how much energy you usually spend preparing for meetings, or will the urge to control the outcome remain strong? Also, how confident do you feel that you can stick with this observation without drifting back into rehearsing the old scripts?

Honestly, I think the urge to control the outcome will still be pretty strong — that's been my habit for so long. But I do feel a little more confident now that I can at least catch myself doing it. Maybe I can write down "just observe" on a sticky note and put it on my desk as a reminder. That is a brilliant solution—using a visual anchor like a sticky note forces your eye to land on reality whenever you feel the urge to drift back into planning mode. Having a gentle reminder outside your head makes it much easier to interrupt that automatic pilot.

To seal this in, how would you rate your confidence from zero to ten on a scale of one being "I won't try it" and ten being "I'll handle whatever comes up"? Where does that landing spot fall for this upcoming experiment?

I'd say maybe a six or seven. That's higher than I would have guessed before we talked, actually. I think having a clear, simple goal — just observe — makes it feel doable, even if my anxiety tries to take over. And the sticky note will help me stay grounded. I'm willing to give it a real try.

A solid six or seven shows real growth, especially considering how high that number usually lands for you on its own. Carrying that note with you acts like a compass, reminding you to trust the data you gather rather than the story your anxiety spins.

Now that we have this plan locked in, is there anything else you'd like to discuss before we finish our time together today?

No, I think this is enough for today. I feel like I have something concrete to work with, which is more than I had when I walked in. Thank you for listening and for helping me see that fuzzy prediction for what it is. I'll let you know how the observation goes next time.

That is wonderful news to hear—knowing you walk away with a concrete tool instead of just advice means a lot. Remember that observation isn't about proving yourself perfect; it's simply gathering fresh data points to challenge that old story.

Please come back soon to tell me exactly what happened at work and whether that sticky note helped bring you back to the present moment. Until then, take care of yourself and trust that you have everything you need to navigate this day.

Ten minutes is a fantastic target—it gives your brain enough time to start quieting down without requiring perfect endurance right away. I actually pretended I didn't hear them. I just stared at the coffee machine like it was the most interesting thing in the world. My hands were shaking a little, and I could feel my face getting hot. That rapid retreat to hide feels like a desperate attempt to prove the opposite of what your boss told you—you weren't hiding because you failed, but because you feared exposure. You're absolutely right—that comparison acts like fuel, instantly inflaming the fire whenever you see someone else thriving or recall even a minor stumble. It creates a false benchmark where you believe your value is tied entirely to fitting into someone else's definition of success. Now that we've traced how it borrows strength from outside comparisons and inside mistakes, I wonder if you could identify one specific piece of evidence from that day in the breakroom that directly contradicts the idea that "you shouldn't be here"? Perhaps noticing your coworkers' normal reactions afterward, or realizing you finished your task successfully later? I mean, I did finish a pretty complex report that afternoon, and my manager actually complimented me on it. It was a good piece of work. You are absolutely correct—the voice is expertly designed to minimize that praise, convincing you that one report doesn't define your entire career trajectory or future potential. I guess... when you put it that way, it does feel a little heavier, like it's not just nothing. Maybe I'm so focused on the cover of the book that I forget there are chapters inside. You have hit on a powerful insight: treating your achievements as isolated events versus parts of a larger story changes everything about how they weigh in. Shifting that expectation from "missing pages equal failure" to "blank pages represent potential" is a huge leap, and it shows real growth in how you're framing uncertainty. I just tried it in my head, picturing the breakroom and saying that line about Chapter One. The heat in my chest is still there, but it's not as sharp. That is such a significant breakthrough; creating space for even a "second voice" proves you are gaining control over the narrative, however small the step may seem. The fact that that new thought reduced the intensity from a "burn" to a "warm discomfort" means you've successfully activated a different neural pathway in your brain. Now that we've practiced shifting the perspective on that specific memory, let's lock in a concrete strategy for tomorrow morning when you walk through the doors. Can we agree to carry that "Chapter One" phrase silently as soon as your feet touch the threshold, reminding yourself that the story is yours to write at your own pace?

Yes, I think I can try that. I'll say it to myself as I walk through the doors tomorrow morning. "This is just Chapter One." It feels a little silly, but maybe that's okay. I've been letting the other voice run things for too long. It's worth a shot to give this new thought a chance.

That humility is incredibly brave, and I completely agree—even sounding "silly" often means a thought is fresh enough to challenge old patterns. Giving that new phrase a chance doesn't mean ignoring the fear entirely; it just means carrying a compass pointing toward possibility alongside the map of past fears. For tonight, before bed, could you review what worked best about that morning rehearsal and decide whether you want to tweak the timing of when you whisper that phrase, or leave it exactly as is? I think I'll keep it as is, first thing when I walk through the door. That's when the feeling hits me hardest, so that's when I need it most. I don't want to overthink it and mess it up. I'll just say it, even if it feels strange.

That simplicity is perfect—you trust your intuition enough to act without needing perfect timing. The visualization feels a little daunting, honestly. I can see myself walking through the door, but the old voice is still there, waiting. That honest acknowledgment—that the old voice will still be there—is actually a great sign, because it means you aren't expecting perfection, just presence. Your ability to recognize the second voice becoming slightly louder shows your brain is starting to learn a new language, even if the translation feels clunky at first. No, I think we're good for now. I'm going to try it tomorrow and see what happens. I'll make a note of how it feels, and we can talk about it next time. Thank you for helping me see that blank page as something other than a failure. That's... that's new for me.

That combination of words and touch sounds powerful enough to ground you right when the anxiety spikes. That assumption—that total silence equals invisibility—is such a strong belief to hold onto when you're feeling vulnerable, especially after years of facing difficult circumstances alone. That fear of abandonment is so intense it feels safer to pretend you are necessary to her existence, even though the proof suggests otherwise. Can we try a tiny experiment right now? That window seat sounds perfect because it turns a habitual spot for distraction into a sanctuary for presence. I think the silence might be too loud at first. Maybe I'll put on some soft music, something without words. Just to ease into it. It feels less daunting that way, like I'm not jumping into a cold pool but wading in slowly. Thank you for suggesting that—I think I can actually try this.

Okay, I'll do that. The hand on my chest part sounds a little silly, but I'm willing to try anything at this point. I'll text you tomorrow and let you know how it went. Thanks for giving me a concrete thing to hold onto tonight, instead of just spiraling.

That distinction perfectly illustrates what psychologists call the "inner critic" versus a supportive friend; you're applying an impossible standard to yourself while naturally offering empathy to others in similar positions. Since you admitted that logic works for a junior dev but fails for you, could you trace back one more step to identify the core belief driving that harshness? Is it truly that you lack knowledge, or is it deeper than that, perhaps suggesting that being seen as flawed means you are inherently unsafe? That fear of becoming a fraud after showing a flaw is incredibly painful, and it explains why protecting that fragile image becomes so urgent for you. Honestly, imagining that scenario does make me pause. I guess there's a small part of me that knows most people wouldn't actually tear me down over a single imperfect idea. So maybe the crumbling feeling is more about my own expectations than what would actually happen.

That realization that others likely tolerate imperfections just like you do offers crucial counter-evidence to your fear of exposure. It shifts the narrative from being personally targeted to simply navigating normal human collaboration. Now, if we accept for a moment that one slightly rough idea won't erase your years of competence, what might replace that immediate panic with something slightly calmer? Could we try labeling that intense physical sensation—a tight chest or rapid heartbeat—as "anticipatory stress" rather than proof of failure? Does naming it physically help create a tiny bit of distance between you and the thought?

Yeah, I think calling it "anticipatory stress" makes sense. When I focus on the physical feeling—the tightness in my chest—I can kind of separate it from the story I tell myself about being a fraud. It's just a body reaction, not a fact. Maybe if I practice noticing that sensation without immediately judging it, I could give myself a second to decide whether to speak up instead of just shutting down.

That separation of the physical sensation from the catastrophic story is exactly the goal we want to achieve. You're describing a powerful technique called grounding, which allows you to observe your nervous system activating without letting it drive the car automatically.

To put this into action right now, let's try a quick simulation: I'll read a hypothetical statement you might overhear in a meeting, and I want you to practice identifying that tight chest as "stress" rather than accepting the "fraud" label immediately. Here we go—"Hey, I noticed that dashboard metric has doubled compared to last month; curious if anyone wants to run a deeper analysis?" What happens in your body during that moment before you jump to conclusions?

Okay, so I'm imagining that statement, and I feel that familiar little flutter in my chest—like a quick jolt. But this time, instead of thinking "I don't know how to run that analysis, I'm out of my depth," I'm trying to just notice the flutter and say to myself, "That's just stress, not a sign I'm incompetent." Noticing that tiny pause and renaming the sensation is exactly what builds the neural pathway for safety over time. That brief interruption gives your conscious mind a chance to choose a different response instead of running on autopilot. Now that we've practiced spotting that pattern and creating space within it, let's agree on a simple plan for tomorrow: whenever you feel that flutter rising in that situation, will you silently whisper "just stress" to ground yourself for three seconds before deciding what to say?

I think I can try that. Three seconds of just saying "just stress" in my head seems manageable—it's not too big a commitment. And if I can do that even once tomorrow, it might prove to myself that I can stop the spiral before it takes over. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That commitment is wonderful because proving to yourself that you can interrupt a spiral is far more valuable than successfully leading a major presentation. Taking that small, three-second break creates a critical window where your rational mind can take over from your fear-driven instinct.

Let's finalize our closing agreement: Your homework is to practice that "just stress" mantra whenever you feel that flutter tomorrow, observing it closely without adding judgments.
